Distance learning has moved from the margins of education to the mainstream, and many schools now allow students to attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing. While traditional classrooms offer real advantages, I believe students would benefit from having distance learning available as an option, because it provides flexibility, supports students with particular needs, and prepares young people for a world in which remote work and study are increasingly common.

The most obvious benefit of distance learning is flexibility. Not every student's life fits neatly into a school timetable. Some teenagers work part-time jobs to support their families, while others care for younger siblings or elderly relatives. For these students, a rigid schedule can mean the difference between staying in school and dropping out. Online classes, especially those that offer recorded lessons, allow students to learn at times that suit their circumstances. Rather than forcing students to choose between responsibility and education, distance learning lets them pursue both.

Distance learning also serves students whose needs are not always met in a traditional classroom. Students with chronic illnesses or physical disabilities may find it difficult to attend school every day, and they often fall behind through no fault of their own. Similarly, some students experience severe anxiety or bullying that makes the school environment harmful rather than helpful. Learning from home can give these students a safe, comfortable space in which they are able to focus on their studies. In addition, students who learn more quickly or more slowly than their peers can move at their own pace, rewatching lessons when they need to or advancing when they are ready.

Finally, distance learning helps prepare students for the future. Many workplaces now rely on video meetings, shared documents, and online collaboration. Students who learn to manage their time, communicate clearly in writing, and stay motivated without constant supervision are developing exactly the skills that employers value. These habits of independence and self-discipline will serve them well in college and beyond.

Critics argue that students who learn from home miss out on important social interaction and may struggle to stay motivated. These concerns are valid, but they are reasons to design distance learning carefully, not reasons to reject it. Schools can include group projects, live discussions, and regular check-ins with teachers, and students can still take part in sports, clubs, and other activities.

In conclusion, distance learning should be offered as an option because it gives students flexibility, supports those with special circumstances, and builds valuable skills. When used thoughtfully, it can make education more accessible for everyone.

Honestly, I think being able to do classes from home would be a good thing for a lot of students, but maybe not for everyone. Like, it really depends on the person and what's going on in their life.

First of all, think about how early school starts. I have to wake up at like 6 in the morning to catch the bus, and half the time I'm basically asleep in first period anyway. If I could log in from home, I'd actually be awake and paying attention instead of just staring at the board. Plus I wouldn't waste almost an hour every day just getting to school and back. That's time I could use to do homework or work or just sleep, which teenagers actually need.

Another thing is that some kids have stuff going on that teachers don't really see. My friend has to babysit her little brothers a lot because her mom works nights, and sometimes she just can't make it to school. If she could do her classes online, she wouldn't keep falling behind and getting in trouble for absences. Also there are kids who get bullied or have anxiety really bad, and for them school is honestly kind of a nightmare. Doing classes from home could help them focus on learning instead of worrying about who's going to say something to them in the hallway.

Online classes also let you go at your own speed. In a normal class, if you don't get something, the teacher just keeps going and you're lost. But if the lesson is recorded, you can pause it and watch it again until it makes sense. That's way better than being too embarrassed to raise your hand.

But I'll admit there are some downsides. It would be really easy to just not pay attention at home, especially if your phone is right there. And you'd miss seeing your friends, which is honestly one of the best parts of school. Some people need a teacher right there to keep them on track, and online school wouldn't work for them.

So overall I think schools should give students the choice. Not everyone has to do it, but for people who need it or learn better that way, it could really help. School is supposed to help everyone learn, and if online classes help some kids do that, then why not?

The question of whether students should be able to attend classes from home has become more pressing as technology has made online learning widely available. Although distance learning offers convenience, I believe most students would not benefit from attending school primarily from home, because in-person schooling provides social development, immediate support from teachers, and a structured environment that online classes struggle to replicate.

School is not only a place where students learn academic content; it is also where they learn how to interact with other people. Through daily conversations, group projects, sports, and even disagreements, students develop communication skills, empathy, and the ability to work as part of a team. These skills are difficult to build through a screen. A video call cannot fully replace the experience of sitting beside a classmate, sharing ideas, and solving a problem together. Students who spend most of their time learning alone at home risk becoming isolated, and research has linked isolation among young people to higher levels of anxiety and depression.

In-person classes also allow teachers to respond to students immediately. A skilled teacher can notice when a student looks confused, pause to explain a concept another way, or offer encouragement at the right moment. In an online class, these signals are easy to miss. Students may hesitate to interrupt a video lesson or may wait hours for an email reply, by which time they have fallen further behind. For students who already find school challenging, this delay can make a significant difference.

Furthermore, the structure of a school day helps many students stay focused. At school, there is a clear schedule, a dedicated space for learning, and fewer distractions. At home, students face constant temptations, from phones and video games to household noise and responsibilities. Not every student has a quiet place to work or a reliable internet connection, which means that distance learning can actually widen the gap between students from different backgrounds.

Supporters of distance learning point out that it offers flexibility for students who are ill, who work, or who have other obligations. This is a fair point, and online options can be valuable as a temporary or supplementary measure in these situations. However, flexibility for some should not come at the cost of the social, academic, and structural benefits that in-person school provides for most.

In conclusion, while distance learning can play a useful supporting role, students generally benefit more from attending school in person. The classroom offers connection, guidance, and structure that are essential to a well-rounded education.

So the question is whether students would benefit from doing school from home, and I kind of have mixed feelings about it, but I think in the end it's not a great idea for most kids.

When we had to do online school for a while, it sounded amazing at first. No waking up early, no bus, you could literally do class in your pajamas. But after like two weeks it got really boring and honestly kind of depressing. You're just sitting in your room staring at a screen all day, and nobody turns their camera on, so it's like talking to a bunch of black squares. I missed just hanging out with my friends at lunch and even the dumb stuff like walking between classes.

Also it's way harder to learn when the teacher isn't right there. If you're confused in a real class you can just ask, or the teacher can tell you're lost by looking at your face. Online you have to unmute and interrupt everyone, which is awkward, so most people just don't. Then you end up trying to figure it out by yourself at 11pm and it doesn't make sense. My grades actually went down when we were online, and a lot of my friends said the same thing.

And let's be real, it's super easy to get distracted at home. Your phone is right there, your bed is right there, your little sister is yelling in the next room. At school there's at least some structure, like you know you're supposed to be working. At home it's way too easy to just open another tab and watch videos while the teacher is talking.

I get that some people really need it though. If you're sick for a long time or you have to work to help your family, then online classes could be really helpful. So maybe it should be an option for those people. But for normal students like me, I think going to actual school is better because you learn more and you actually get to be around people.

So yeah, I don't think most students would benefit that much from doing classes from home. It sounds good but it's not as fun or easy as people think.

As online technology continues to improve, many schools have begun offering distance learning as an alternative to traditional classes. I believe that students can benefit significantly from being able to attend classes from home, provided that schools offer it as a choice rather than a requirement. Distance learning increases access to education, allows students to learn in ways that suit them, and helps them develop independence.

One of the strongest arguments for distance learning is that it makes education more accessible. Students who live in rural areas may face long journeys to school every day, while others may not have reliable transport at all. Students who are recovering from illness or injury, or who live with long-term health conditions, often miss weeks of learning. Distance learning removes many of these barriers. As long as a student has a device and an internet connection, they can attend lessons, submit work, and stay connected to their teachers, regardless of where they are.

Distance learning also allows students to learn in the way that works best for them. In a traditional classroom, lessons move at a single pace, which can leave some students bored and others struggling. Online courses often include recorded lectures, interactive exercises, and digital resources that students can revisit as often as they need. A student who finds mathematics difficult can replay a lesson several times, while a student who has already mastered a topic can move on. This personalized approach can lead to deeper understanding and greater confidence.

In addition, attending classes from home encourages students to become more independent and responsible. Without a teacher constantly supervising them, students must learn to plan their time, meet deadlines, and motivate themselves. These are essential skills for college and for many modern careers, where people are increasingly expected to work remotely and manage their own schedules.

Of course, distance learning is not perfect. Some students may feel lonely or find it hard to concentrate at home, and not every family can afford a computer or fast internet. Schools must address these challenges by providing devices, maintaining regular contact with students, and creating opportunities for online collaboration and social interaction.

Overall, the benefits of distance learning outweigh its drawbacks when it is offered as an option. By giving students more ways to learn, schools can ensure that more young people succeed, no matter what obstacles they face.

I think students should definitely be able to take classes from home if they want to. Not everybody learns the same way, and regular school just doesn't work for some people.

For example, I'm the kind of person who gets distracted really easily in class. There's always someone talking or tapping their pencil or doing something annoying, and I can't focus. When I do my homework at home in my room with my music on, I actually get way more done. So if I could take some of my classes from home, I think I'd learn better and my grades would probably go up.

Another reason is that school takes up so much time that isn't even learning. Think about it. You spend like 20 minutes in homeroom doing nothing, then 5 minutes between every class, then lunch, then waiting for the bus. If you add it all up that's hours every day. With online classes you could just do the actual learning part and then have time for other things like a job or sports or helping out at home.

Also some kids just have a really hard time at school because of other people. There's a kid in my grade who gets picked on basically every day, and you can tell he hates being there. If he could do school from home he could just focus on his work and not have to deal with all that. School should be about learning, not about surviving.

I know some people say you need to be at school to make friends and learn social skills. But you can still see your friends outside of school, and there's group chats and stuff. And honestly, a lot of the "social skills" you learn at school is just how to deal with drama, which isn't really that useful.

The only problem is that some people would probably just not do their work if they were home. But that's their choice, and the school could check on them. And people who need to be in a classroom could still go to regular school.

So overall I think online classes would really help a lot of students. It gives people more options, and that's never a bad thing.

Few changes in education have been as rapid or as debated as the rise of distance learning. Today, students in many schools can attend lessons through video conferencing or complete entire courses online. While this option has clear advantages in particular circumstances, I believe that, for the majority of students, attending classes from home is less beneficial than learning in a physical classroom. Distance learning weakens relationships, reduces accountability, and deepens existing inequalities.

Learning is fundamentally social. Students learn not only from teachers but from one another, through discussion, debate, and collaboration. In a classroom, a question from one student can spark a conversation that helps the entire class understand a topic more deeply. Online, these exchanges are far less natural. Many students keep their cameras and microphones off, and discussions often become stilted or one-sided. Over time, the relationships between students and between students and teachers become weaker, and those relationships are often what keep young people engaged in school.

Distance learning also makes it harder to hold students accountable. In a classroom, a teacher can see whether students are paying attention and can quickly redirect someone who has drifted off. At home, a student can appear to be present in an online lesson while actually playing games or sleeping. Without consistent supervision, students who struggle with motivation are likely to fall further behind, and teachers may not realize there is a problem until it is too late.

Perhaps most importantly, distance learning can widen the gap between advantaged and disadvantaged students. A student with a quiet bedroom, a fast laptop, and parents who are able to help with schoolwork will usually manage well online. A student who shares a crowded home, relies on a phone for internet access, or has to look after younger siblings during the day will face far greater obstacles. In-person schools, for all their flaws, provide every student with the same building, the same resources, and the same access to teachers.

There are certainly situations in which distance learning is the right choice, such as for students with serious medical conditions or those living in remote areas. In these cases, online classes can be a lifeline. However, these exceptions do not change the fact that most students learn best in person.

In conclusion, schools should keep distance learning as a supplementary option for students with specific needs, but in-person classes should remain the norm. The classroom offers the relationships, accountability, and equal access that every student deserves.

Should students be able to go to school from home? I think yes, but only some of the time, not all of the time. Like maybe a mix of both would be the best.

The good thing about online classes is you have way more freedom. You don't have to sit in a hard desk for seven hours, you can take a break when you need one, and you can eat whenever you're hungry instead of waiting for lunch. I feel like I'd be a lot less stressed if I didn't have to deal with the whole school routine every single day. Also if you're sick you could still do your classes instead of missing a bunch of work and having to make it all up later, which is the worst.

But there's also a lot of stuff you'd miss out on. Like science labs, you can't really do those at home unless you want to blow up your kitchen. And gym class, and art, and band. Those are some of the only classes I actually look forward to, and you can't do them over a computer. Plus seeing your friends every day is a big part of why school is even bearable.

Another problem is not everyone has good internet. At my cousin's house the wifi is so slow that videos barely load, so online school would be really hard for her. It wouldn't be fair if some kids couldn't even get into class because their internet sucks.

That's why I think a mix would work best. Maybe students could go to school three days a week and do the other two days online. That way you still get to see people and do the hands-on stuff, but you also get some days where you can sleep in a little and work at your own pace. Teachers could put the lectures online and then use the days at school for projects and questions.

I think that would make school a lot better for most students. Some people learn better at home and some learn better at school, so having both would help everyone. Students would benefit from having the option, as long as they don't have to give up the parts of school that are actually good.

Advances in technology have made it possible for students to attend classes without ever entering a school building. Video conferencing, online learning platforms, and digital textbooks mean that a student can now follow an entire curriculum from home. I believe that students would benefit from having this option, because it allows them to balance education with other responsibilities, reduces the stress that many experience at school, and gives them greater control over how they learn.

Many students carry responsibilities that extend well beyond the classroom. Some work to support their families, others care for relatives, and some are training seriously in sports or the arts. For these students, the fixed hours of a traditional school day can be a major obstacle. Distance learning offers a solution by allowing students to complete lessons at times that suit them. A student who works in the afternoon could attend live classes in the morning and complete assignments in the evening, ensuring that they do not have to give up their education to meet their other obligations.

School can also be a source of considerable stress. Crowded hallways, social pressure, and in some cases bullying can make it difficult for students to focus on learning. For students who experience anxiety or who have been the target of harassment, simply walking into school each day can be exhausting. Learning from home can provide a calmer environment in which these students are able to concentrate and rebuild their confidence. When students feel safe, they are far more likely to succeed academically.

In addition, distance learning gives students more control over their education. Recorded lessons can be paused and replayed, allowing students to review difficult concepts as many times as necessary. Online resources make it easy to explore topics in greater depth or to seek extra help. Students who take responsibility for their own learning in this way often develop stronger study habits and greater independence, qualities that will benefit them in higher education and in the workplace.

Some people worry that students who learn from home will become isolated or lose motivation. These risks are real, but they can be reduced through regular contact with teachers, virtual group work, and participation in extracurricular activities. Distance learning does not have to mean learning alone.

In conclusion, offering distance learning as an option would benefit many students by giving them flexibility, reducing stress, and encouraging independence. Schools that embrace this opportunity will be better able to meet the needs of every learner.

Okay so I've actually thought about this a lot because my older brother did online school for his last two years of high school. And from what I saw, I think it can be good for some people, but it's definitely not for everyone.

For my brother it worked really well. He was really into robotics and he had a part-time job at a computer repair shop, and regular school was just taking up too much of his time. With online school he could do his classes in the morning, go to work in the afternoon, and still have time for his robotics stuff at night. He actually graduated early. So for someone like him who knows what they want and is good at managing their time, online school is honestly great.

But I also saw how hard it was sometimes. There were days where he just didn't feel like doing anything and nobody was there to make him. He got behind a couple times and had to stay up super late catching up. And he said he kind of missed having teachers that actually knew him. Online the teachers have like a hundred students and they don't really know who you are.

I don't think I would do well with online school, to be honest. I need people around me to stay motivated. When I see everyone else working in class it makes me want to work too. At home I would probably just end up on my phone the whole day. Also I would really miss my friends and stuff like football games and school dances.

So I think the answer is that students would benefit from being able to choose. If you're like my brother and you're responsible and have other things going on, online classes could help you a lot. But if you're like me and you need structure, you should go to regular school. Schools should let students pick what works best for them instead of forcing everyone to do the same thing.

In the end, school is supposed to help you get ready for your future, and everybody's future looks different. Having more options would help more students succeed.

Distance learning, in which students attend classes online or through video conferencing, is now offered by a growing number of schools. Although it is sometimes presented as the future of education, I believe that students benefit more from attending school in person. Physical classrooms support mental health, provide practical learning opportunities, and create a sense of community that online classes cannot match.

The mental health of young people is closely tied to their connections with others. School provides daily contact with friends, teachers, and mentors, and these relationships offer support during difficult times. When students learn from home, many of these connections fade. Experiences during periods of widespread remote learning showed that many students felt lonely, anxious, and disconnected. While online classes can deliver information, they cannot easily provide the sense of belonging that comes from being part of a school community.

In-person schooling also offers practical learning experiences that are difficult to reproduce online. Science experiments, art projects, music ensembles, physical education, and technical subjects all require equipment, space, and hands-on guidance. A student cannot learn to use laboratory equipment safely or play in an orchestra through a screen. Even in academic subjects, face-to-face discussion and collaborative problem-solving help students think critically and learn from different perspectives.

Moreover, schools are communities that teach values and responsibilities beyond the curriculum. Students learn to respect rules, resolve conflicts, and contribute to something larger than themselves, whether through student government, sports teams, or volunteer projects. These experiences help shape responsible citizens. When students spend their school years at home, they miss many of the opportunities that help them grow into confident, capable adults.

Supporters of distance learning argue that it offers flexibility and can help students who face obstacles to attending school. This is true, and for some students, online learning can be an important alternative. However, the needs of a minority should be addressed through targeted programs rather than by encouraging all students to learn from home.

In conclusion, while distance learning has a place in modern education, it should not replace the traditional classroom for most students. Attending school in person supports students' well-being, provides valuable practical experience, and builds the sense of community that is essential to a complete education.

The Facial Action Coding System, described in the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile," allows computers to analyze the movements of facial muscles and identify human emotions. Its developers suggest that the technology could be used in classrooms to detect when students are confused or bored. While this idea is innovative, I do not believe that using this technology to read students' emotional expressions is valuable, because it raises serious privacy concerns, may be inaccurate, and could undermine the relationship between teachers and students.

First, using emotion-recognition software in classrooms would raise significant privacy issues. Students' emotions are personal, and many young people would feel uncomfortable knowing that a computer was constantly monitoring their faces. Unlike a teacher who notices a student's mood in passing, a computer could record and store detailed data about every expression a student makes. This information could potentially be misused or shared without students' consent. Schools should be places where students feel safe, not places where they feel watched.

Second, the technology may not be as accurate as it seems. The article explains that the software compares a person's expression to a neutral face and calculates the percentage of each emotion. However, facial expressions vary greatly between individuals and cultures. A student who naturally looks serious might be labeled as bored or upset when they are actually concentrating. A student who is struggling with problems at home might be flagged as confused about the lesson. If teachers rely on these readings, they could make incorrect assumptions about their students.

Third, relying on technology to interpret emotions could weaken the human connection that is central to good teaching. Experienced teachers already observe their students closely and know when someone needs help. More importantly, they can talk with students, ask questions, and build trust. A computer program cannot replace the understanding that comes from a genuine relationship. If students know that a machine is tracking their feelings, they may become less willing to share how they truly feel.

Supporters argue that the software could help adapt lessons to students' needs, much like an effective human instructor. While this goal is admirable, it can be achieved through better teacher training, smaller class sizes, and open communication.

In conclusion, although the Facial Action Coding System is an impressive scientific achievement, its use in classrooms is not valuable. The risks to privacy, the potential for inaccuracy, and the threat to human relationships outweigh the possible benefits.

In the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile," it talks about this new technology called the Facial Action Coding System that can tell what emotions people are feeling just by looking at their face. They want to use it in classrooms so the computer can tell if students are bored or confused. I think it's kind of a cool idea but I don't really think it would be that useful in school.

First of all, it's honestly kind of creepy. Imagine sitting in class and knowing there's a computer watching your face the whole time and figuring out how you feel. I wouldn't like that at all. Sometimes you just have a bad day and you don't want anyone to know about it, especially not a computer that might tell your teacher. Your feelings should be private.

Second, I don't think it would even be that accurate. The article says the computer figured out that the Mona Lisa was 83 percent happy and 9 percent disgusted and stuff like that. But how does it really know? Some people just have a face that looks mad even when they're not. My friend always looks bored but she's actually one of the smartest people in our class and she's usually paying attention. If the computer kept saying she was bored, the teacher might think she isn't trying when she really is.

Third, teachers can already tell when students are confused. Good teachers look around the room and can see when people don't get it. And if you're confused you can just raise your hand and ask. We don't need a whole expensive computer program to do something teachers can already do. The school could use that money for something better, like new books or fixing the air conditioning.

I guess one good thing is that it might help with online classes, because the teacher can't really see your face that well over video. And the article says it could make video games better, which would be cool. But for regular classrooms I don't think it's needed.

So overall, I don't think using this technology in classrooms is that valuable. It's creepy, it might not be accurate, and teachers can already do what it does. Some things should just be left to people instead of computers.

In "Making Mona Lisa Smile," the author describes the Facial Action Coding System, a technology that enables computers to identify human emotions by analyzing the movements of the face's muscles. Dr. Thomas Huang and his colleagues suggest that this technology could transform the classroom by allowing computers to recognize when students are confused or bored. I believe that using this technology to read students' emotional expressions is valuable, because it could help teachers personalize instruction, identify students who are struggling, and improve online learning.

The most significant benefit of the technology is that it could help personalize learning. In a typical classroom, one teacher is responsible for twenty or thirty students, each with different needs. It is impossible for a teacher to notice every moment when a student begins to lose interest or becomes confused. According to the article, "a classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored," and then "modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor." This means that a student who is struggling could receive additional explanation, while a student who is bored could be given a more challenging task. Such responsiveness could help every student learn more effectively.

The technology could also help identify students who are experiencing emotional difficulties. Some students hide their problems well, and teachers may not realize that a student is anxious, sad, or overwhelmed. Because the software can detect even mixed emotions, it could alert teachers to students who might need support. Early intervention can make a significant difference in a young person's well-being and academic success.

In addition, the Facial Action Coding System could greatly improve online learning. When students learn through a screen, teachers lose many of the visual cues they would normally rely on. Emotion-recognition software could restore some of that awareness, helping online teachers understand how their students are responding to a lesson. As more education moves online, this ability will become increasingly important.

Some people may worry about privacy, and these concerns deserve careful attention. Schools would need clear rules about how emotional data is collected, stored, and used. However, with appropriate safeguards, the benefits of the technology could be achieved without compromising students' rights.

In conclusion, the Facial Action Coding System has the potential to make classrooms more responsive and supportive. By helping teachers understand their students' emotions, it could improve both learning and well-being, making it a valuable tool for education.

So the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile" is about this technology that can read your emotions by looking at the muscles in your face. The scientists think it could be used in classrooms to see if students are confused or bored. I actually think this could be pretty helpful, even though some people might think it's weird.

I know some people would say it's an invasion of privacy, and I kind of get that. Nobody wants to feel like they're being watched all the time. The article "Making Mona Lisa Smile" introduces the Facial Action Coding System, a technology that allows computers to recognize emotions by tracking the movements of the forty-four major muscles of the human face. The author suggests that such a system could help classroom computers detect when students are confused or bored. Although the technology is fascinating, I believe its use to read students' emotions in the classroom would be of limited value, because emotions are complex, students deserve autonomy, and the cost would be difficult to justify.

Human emotions are far more complex than a set of percentages. The software famously calculated that the Mona Lisa was 83 percent happy, 9 percent disgusted, 6 percent fearful, and 2 percent angry. While this is an entertaining demonstration, it oversimplifies what people actually feel. A student might frown because they are concentrating hard on a difficult problem, not because they are confused or unhappy. Another might smile politely while feeling completely lost. Reducing these complex states to numbers risks misleading teachers rather than informing them.

Furthermore, students deserve some control over how much of themselves they share. Adolescence is a time when young people are learning to manage their feelings and to decide what to reveal to others. Constant emotional monitoring would take that choice away. Students who know they are being observed may feel pressure to perform certain emotions, such as appearing interested at all times, which could increase stress rather than improve learning. A classroom should be a place where students feel free to think, not a place where their faces are constantly evaluated.

Finally, schools have limited budgets, and installing emotion-recognition software on every classroom computer would be expensive. The money required to purchase, maintain, and secure such systems could instead be spent on hiring more teachers, reducing class sizes, or providing counseling services. These investments would directly address the problems the technology aims to solve, such as students who feel confused or disengaged, and would do so through human relationships rather than surveillance.

It is true that the technology could have useful applications in other fields, such as making animated characters more realistic or helping researchers understand emotional expression. Its value in those areas, however, does not automatically extend to the classroom.

In conclusion, while the Facial Action Coding System represents an impressive scientific advance, using it to read students' emotions in class would offer limited benefits. Teachers and counselors, not computers, are best placed to understand and support students.

The article "Making Mona Lisa Smile" explains how computers can now read people's emotions using something called the Facial Action Coding System. Dr. Huang thinks it could be used in classrooms to help teachers know when students are bored or confused. I think this idea is valuable, but only if it is used carefully.

One reason I think it's valuable is because teachers have so many students that they can't keep track of everyone. In my English class there's like 32 people, and the teacher can't possibly look at all of us at the same time. Some people just fall through the cracks. If a computer could help the teacher notice who's struggling, more students would get the help they need and fewer people would fail.

Another reason is that it could help students understand their own emotions. Sometimes I feel stressed or frustrated but I don't really realize it until later. If the program could show me how I'm feeling, it might help me take a break or calm down before I get too overwhelmed. The article also talks about how making facial expressions can actually change how you feel, which is kind of interesting. Maybe the technology could help people feel better.

But there are definitely some problems. The biggest one is privacy. I wouldn't want a computer saving data about my emotions all day. When people face an important decision, many of them seek advice from more than one person. Some might ask why this is necessary when one trusted friend or expert could simply tell them what to do. However, seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice, because it provides a wider range of perspectives, helps reveal hidden risks, and allows the person to recognize patterns in the advice they receive.

First, asking several people for advice exposes a person to a variety of perspectives. Everyone sees a situation through the lens of their own experiences, values, and knowledge. A parent might focus on safety, a teacher on long-term goals, and a friend on what will make someone happy right now. For example, a student deciding whether to take an advanced class might hear from a parent that it will strengthen college applications, from a teacher that it requires significant time, and from an older student that it was stressful but rewarding. Each perspective adds something important, and together they give the student a much more complete picture than any single opinion could.

Second, multiple opinions can help reveal risks or problems that one person might overlook. No adviser knows everything. Someone considering buying a used car, for instance, might ask a friend who loves the model, but a mechanic might point out a common mechanical problem, and a relative might warn about high insurance costs. By gathering advice from different sources, a person is less likely to be blindsided by an issue that only one adviser was aware of.

Third, when a person hears similar advice from several people, they can feel more confident in their decision. If three different people independently suggest the same course of action, it is likely to be a sound choice. On the other hand, if the advice is divided, the person knows that the decision is genuinely difficult and can take more time to think it through carefully. In either case, comparing opinions helps the person understand the strength of the arguments on each side.

Of course, asking too many people can sometimes cause confusion, and in the end the decision belongs to the person making it. Seeking advice is not about letting others decide; it is about gathering information so that one's own judgment is better informed.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions helps people make better choices by broadening their perspective, uncovering hidden risks, and building confidence. When an important decision is at stake, listening to more than one voice is a wise approach.

In the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the author explores both the promise and the problems of self-driving vehicles. After considering the evidence, I believe that the development of driverless cars should continue, because they have the potential to save lives, increase independence for many people, and make transportation more efficient, provided that safety and legal questions are carefully addressed.

The most compelling argument for driverless cars is their potential to improve safety. The vast majority of car accidents are caused by human error, such as distraction, fatigue, speeding, or impaired driving. A well-designed autonomous system does not text, fall asleep, or drink alcohol. It can monitor its surroundings in every direction at once and react faster than a human driver. If driverless technology can reduce even a fraction of these errors, thousands of lives could be saved every year.

Driverless cars could also give greater independence to people who are currently unable to drive. Elderly people who can no longer drive safely, people with disabilities, and others who cannot obtain a license often depend on family members or limited public transportation. Self-driving cars could allow them to travel to work, medical appointments, and social events on their own. This independence would greatly improve their quality of life.

In addition, driverless cars could make transportation more efficient. The article describes how the technology could lead to systems in which cars communicate with one another, reducing traffic congestion and fuel use. Cars could travel closer together safely, choose the most efficient routes, and even be shared among multiple users, reducing the total number of vehicles on the road.

The author also raises valid concerns. Current technology still requires a human driver to remain alert and ready to take control, which limits its usefulness. There are also difficult legal questions about who should be responsible if a driverless car causes an accident: the driver, the manufacturer, or the software developer. These issues are serious, but they are reasons to develop the technology carefully, not reasons to abandon it. New laws, rigorous testing, and gradual introduction can address these challenges over time.

In conclusion, the development of driverless cars should move forward. Although the technology is not yet perfect, its potential to save lives, increase independence, and improve efficiency makes it worth pursuing. With careful regulation and continued improvement, driverless cars could transform transportation for the better.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support changing the way we elect the President of the United States from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. Although the Electoral College has a long history, it no longer serves the needs of a modern democracy. A popular vote would ensure that every vote counts equally, encourage candidates to campaign across the entire country, and strengthen public trust in our elections.

The most important reason to adopt a popular vote is that it treats every voter equally. Under the current system, the President is not chosen directly by the people but by 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Because most states award all of their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state, millions of votes effectively do not affect the outcome. A voter in a state that is safely won by one party has far less influence than a voter in a closely divided state. In several elections, including the election of 2000, the candidate who received the most votes nationwide did not become President. In a democracy, the candidate chosen by the most people should win.

A national popular vote would also encourage candidates to pay attention to the entire country. Currently, candidates focus their time, money, and attention on a small number of "swing states," while largely ignoring states they are certain to win or lose. As a result, the concerns of voters in many states receive little attention during campaigns. If every vote counted equally, candidates would have a reason to listen to people everywhere, from large cities to small rural towns.

Finally, moving to a popular vote would strengthen trust in our democracy. When the outcome of an election contradicts the popular vote, many citizens feel that the system is unfair, and some lose faith in the value of voting at all. A simple, transparent system in which the candidate with the most votes wins would be easier to understand and harder to dispute.

Supporters of the Electoral College argue that it protects smaller states and encourages candidates to build broad coalitions. These goals are important, but the current system does not truly achieve them, since most small states are ignored unless they happen to be competitive.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask you to support electing the President by popular vote. Doing so would make our elections fairer, more inclusive, and more democratic.

Sincerely,
A concerned citizen

Okay, I know you really believe that the Face on Mars was made by aliens, and I get why. When you look at that first picture from 1976, it really does look like a giant face staring up from the ground. But as a NASA scientist, I'm going to explain why it's actually just a natural landform, and I think once you hear the evidence you'll agree with me.

First of all, you have to remember how bad the cameras were back then. The Viking 1 picture from 1976 was really blurry, and each pixel covered about 43 meters. That means a lot of small details just got blended together. The shadows made it look like there were eyes, a nose, and a mouth, but that's just how the light hit the rocks at that moment. It's kind of like when you see shapes in clouds.

Second, we went back and took better pictures. In 1998, the Mars Global Surveyor took a photo that was ten times sharper than the Viking one, and guess what? It just looked like a regular rock formation. I know some people said it was cloudy that time, so in 2001 we took another one with the camera at its absolute maximum resolution. Each pixel was only 1.56 meters, so if there was anything like a building or a pyramid, we would have seen it. But there wasn't. It's just a mesa, which is a flat-topped hill.

Third, landforms like this are actually pretty common. There are mesas and buttes all over the American West, like in Idaho, and some of them look kind of like faces or animals too. Nobody thinks aliens made those. The Face on Mars is just the same kind of thing, except it's on another planet.

Also, think about it this way. If NASA really found evidence of aliens, why would we hide it? That would be the biggest discovery ever. We would get so much funding and attention. We would want everyone to know.

So I hope this helps you understand that the Face on Mars is not an alien monument. It's just a natural landform that happened to look like a face in an old blurry picture. The science and the newer photos all prove it.

The Face on Mars is a genuinely mysterious feature, yet it has only been captured clearly on camera once, and that was in the 1970s. The cameras of 1976 were far from sharp: each pixel covered about 43 meters, which made the image considerably blurrier. Although the formation became famous around the world as either an unexplained landform or an alien artifact, the evidence has since been examined closely, and the Face turns out not to be a face at all.

The Face became a popular symbol among alien conspiracy theorists, who believed the photograph offered solid proof that aliens had been at work on Mars. There is a problem, however: that photo was taken in the 1970s, when camera technology was limited. Several more images of the same formation were taken later, in 1998 and in 2001, and rather than showing an Egyptian-style face staring back, they revealed an ordinary, everyday Martian mesa. The 1998 images, taken with a camera ten times sharper than the original Viking camera, clearly showed that the Face was not really a face. Still, the public was not satisfied, arguing that the camera could not capture the Face properly because it was a cloudy season on Mars.

Three years later, scientists photographed the exact location of the original sighting once again, and the camera revealed the same unremarkable rock formation. This time, the press could not argue. The new camera captured 1.56 meters per pixel, compared with the Viking's 43 meters per pixel, and conditions on Mars were as clear as they could be, yet there were no artificial structures to be seen. It is admittedly difficult to prove beyond doubt that the famous mesa is not artificial, since that would require being on the planet itself. Nevertheless, the facts and research are all available, and it is time to let the idea go.

In conclusion, the Face on Mars has had an iconic influence on people and on the world as a whole. It has been analyzed and researched again and again, and the cold, hard facts all point to the same conclusion: the intriguing rock photographed in 1976 is simply a rock formation that was, for now at least, misunderstood.

Cars have been an enormously useful means of transportation, but have they genuinely improved our lives, or have they simply made us too lazy to walk to a friend's house or to school? I believe we could manage perfectly well without them. Like most changes in life, it would simply be a matter of adjusting. Cars have certainly saved us time and made travel more comfortable, yet I feel they are also harming us, because we have fallen into the habit of driving everywhere we go.

People in the United States are beginning to recognize this. By 2013, the number of miles driven per person had fallen nearly 9 percent below its peak, returning to roughly the level the country was at in January 1995. This suggests that some people are starting to drive less, and that we are witnessing a long-term cultural shift.

Without cars, pollution would not affect us nearly as much as it does today, since much of it comes from the fuel that cars burn. Many young people are also losing interest in cars. One reason is that communicating has become much easier: with smartphones, we no longer need to visit a friend's house in person when we can simply use FaceTime or a similar app. For many, a car has become nothing more than a way of getting from point A to point B when public transit is not working.

We can live without cars; it is simply a matter of getting used to it. If we all make a genuine effort, we will actually be helping the world, because pollution will decrease and people will walk to places instead of driving everywhere out of convenience.

There are many advantages to limiting the use of cars. Are there disadvantages as well? Certainly. Limiting cars could even be dangerous, because police, fire departments, and hospitals all depend on vehicles. Police need cars to catch criminals quickly, firefighters need them to rescue us from fires (and to get cats down from trees, though how the cats get up there in the first place remains a mystery), and hospitals need them to bring patients in quickly so doctors can save them. Even so, I personally believe that limiting cars is a great idea.

First of all, many people could lose their jobs if car use were limited, including mechanics and car dealers. Mechanics would lose business, and so would dealerships; if dealers stopped selling many cars, the manufacturers themselves might struggle. However, this pressure could also encourage companies to build better vehicles, such as hybrids, which would reduce pollution and our reliance on fossil fuels. In Vauban, a suburb in Germany, 70 percent of families do not own cars, and 57 percent sold a car in order to move there. As one resident, Heidrun Walter, put it, "When I had a car I was always tense. I'm much happier this way."

Another advantage is that car-free areas are far more peaceful and quiet. In the article "In German Suburb, Life Goes On Without Cars," the author describes how "the swish of bicycles and the chatter of wandering children drown out the occasional distant motor." This shows how calm such places can be: there is little noise, little pollution, and the residents are healthier because they cycle and walk so much, rather than breathing in exhaust fumes. Even the Environmental Protection Agency is promoting "car reduced" communities, and lawmakers are beginning to follow suit.

People without cars tend to walk, cycle, or even run more often, which likely lowers their stress levels. Less stress generally means greater happiness, since exercise relieves tension and can reduce headaches and other health problems. The death rate could also fall, because there would be fewer car accidents, which are a leading cause of death in the United States. In Bogota, a capital city of 7 million people, residents recently held their third annual Day Without Cars, when only buses and taxis were permitted. The goal was to promote alternative transportation and reduce smog, and violators faced $25 fines. Turnout was large despite gray clouds and occasional rain. "The rain hasn't stopped people from participating," said the mayor of Bogota.

In conclusion, the advantages of limiting cars are considerable. People in car-free cities and neighborhoods are happier, healthier, and less stressed. But who will rescue the cats from the trees? Perhaps, without the pollution and frightening engine noise, they will not need to climb them at all.

Limiting car use makes our roads safer and reduces the amount of greenhouse gas in the atmosphere. If more people chose to walk or cycle, local smog levels would fall dramatically. Driving less also saves money on fuel, which can then be spent on other things.

Passenger cars account for 12 percent of greenhouse gas emissions in Europe and up to 50 percent in some parts of the United States. Simply walking to work every other day, or carpooling, can make a substantial difference to the emissions your vehicle produces.

With fewer cars, parking lots could be made smaller, freeing up space for shops and services. Instead of driving five or ten miles to the nearest store, people would find what they need within walking distance. In Bogota, Colombia, which holds an annual car-free day, new parks and sports centers have sprung up, along with restaurants and shopping districts located close to where people live. Driving less also saves a great deal of money. Consider how much you currently spend on fuel; you could cut that cost in half by walking to work every other day or by sharing rides with others. Have you ever wondered what it would be like to take an online class? Learning online requires students to motivate themselves every single day to sit down at a computer and study, which many people find difficult and stressful. Students would not benefit from online classes, because they would be unable to interact with their peers, they would struggle to get help when they need it, and they would lack the motivation to work hard.

Some people would disagree with this position, arguing that online classes would benefit students. For example, many schools began offering online classes because of COVID-19. With students around the world required to stay indoors to prevent the virus from spreading, online classes allowed them to keep learning without leaving home. Nevertheless, there are other viewpoints to consider.

To begin with, online classes would not benefit students, because many students learn by interacting with others. Frederick Douglass, for example, was born into slavery and was not taught to read or write. When he was sent out on errands, he would find local children and play games with them, challenging them to see who could recite the alphabet best. By cleverly turning these games into lessons again and again, he learned to read. Although Douglass was forbidden from learning, he succeeded by learning from the people around him.

In addition, online classes would not benefit students, because when students make mistakes, they want to understand what they did wrong. When Tom Brady throws an interception, for instance, his coach sits down with him and explains the error. Coaches teach their players what to do and what to avoid. Without that coach, Brady would have to rely on an online source, and waiting for a reply could take a long time. That is why, after a game, players and coaches gather in a room to review their mistakes, receiving feedback and support as quickly as possible.

Finally, online classes would not benefit students, because they would lack the motivation to work hard. When I go to school, I draw on the energy around me. I want to see that the people around me are engaged in learning, and that is what motivates me: being surrounded by people who want to learn and succeed as much as I do. That experience simply cannot be replicated in an online class.

In conclusion, online classes would not benefit students, because students would be unable to get help easily, would lack motivation, and would miss out on interaction with their peers. Students would not thrive if they learned only from home. Schools should not adopt this approach, because every student deserves the chance to experience a real classroom and the activities that come with it.

Many students lead busy and varied lives, and some are expected to do far more than simply attend school and complete homework. For these students, attending classes in person can sometimes be difficult. I believe students would benefit greatly from being able to attend classes from home.

Online classes would help students who fall ill and miss school for several days or even a week. When attendance must be in person, sick students miss the classwork, the homework, and the lessons their teachers deliver. If classes were online, these students could watch a recording of each lesson while still getting the rest and care they need, without falling behind.

Other students face family emergencies or unexpected personal situations. Missing several days of school as a result can seriously affect their grades. If they could attend classes online, they would be able to complete their work and follow their teachers' lessons while dealing with the emergency, without the complications of traveling to school or missing days entirely.

Vacations around school breaks and holidays also frequently cause students to miss school. Families sometimes extend their trips, which means their children miss several days of class. If those students were taking online classes, they could bring their schoolwork with them and complete it in the car, while waiting for a flight, or before going to bed. This would help them stay on track so they do not face a mountain of catch-up work when they return.

Students' lives can be very busy, depending on their family circumstances and daily schedules. Attending school in person can be challenging for some, which is why online classes would benefit students so much: they would allow them to continue their education while managing everything else they need to do.

Can computers really understand human emotions? According to the article, using the Facial Action Coding System to read students' emotional expressions in the classroom is valuable because it helps us understand emotions, recognize genuine emotions, and connect with them.

First, the technology helps us understand emotions. According to the article, it can detect mixed emotions. The new emotion-recognition software tracks facial movements, whether in a real face or in the painted face of the Mona Lisa, and it can even tell the difference between a natural smile and a forced one.

Second, the technology allows us to recognize true emotions. The article explains that in a false smile, the mouth is stretched sideways using the zygomatic major muscle, whereas in a genuine smile, the zygomatic major lifts the corners of the mouth. This demonstrates that the technology can distinguish between a sincere smile and an insincere one.

Finally, the technology can help us connect with emotions. The Facial Feedback Theory of Emotion suggests that moving your facial muscles not only expresses emotions but may also help produce them. For example, a drama coach might have students smile and frown so that they can genuinely feel those emotions on stage.

In conclusion, the article shows that using this technology to read students' emotional expressions in a classroom is valuable because it helps us understand emotions, recognize genuine feelings, and connect with them. This matters because some people struggle to read certain emotions, and understanding them better allows us to understand how others feel. It is also important because the better we understand emotions, the more effectively we can use them. For all of these reasons, this technology could be very valuable to students.

I believe using this technology would be a smart idea, because it would allow teachers to tell how students are feeling emotionally, and it could even help make people happier. The software can tell whether a smile is genuine by examining the muscles involved: in a real smile, the cheek muscles lift the corners of the mouth, whereas in a fake smile, the mouth is simply stretched sideways. As the professors put it, faces do not lie.

The facial expressions associated with each emotion are universal, "even though individuals often show varying degrees of expression," such as not smiling as broadly. Using video imagery, the new emotion-recognition software tracks these subtle movements, whether in a real face or in the painted face of the Mona Lisa. By weighing the different action units, the software can even identify mixed emotions. Each expression is compared against a neutral face that shows no emotion. The Mona Lisa demonstration is mainly intended to make people smile, but it also shows just how capable the software is.

Imagine a computer that knows when you are happy or sad. If you smile when a web advertisement appears on your screen, a similar ad might follow, but if you frown, the next one will be different. In the same way, a classroom computer could adjust a lesson, much like an effective human teacher. The same technology could also make computer-animated faces more expressive, for example in video games or video surgery. Since most human communication, including emotional communication, is nonverbal, computers need to understand it too.

But can we really "calculate" emotions, as if they were math homework? And how can a computer recognize the subtle facial movements that people use to express their feelings? The process begins when the computer builds a 3-D model of the face, in which all 44 major muscles must move just like human muscles. The movement of one or more of these muscles is called an "action unit."

"New software has been developed that improves accuracy in perceiving the emotions of others." In my opinion, receiving targeted help from teachers, who can explain the specific steps a student is struggling with, is a much better option.

Second, we do not know how accurate this software really is. The program could be overly sensitive and might mistake confusion for anger. A student could be upset about something unrelated, or might simply have a particular resting expression. The software's usefulness would depend heavily on its accuracy.

Finally, why spend large sums of money installing programs on hundreds of school computers when we can already get help from our teachers? Teachers are there to answer specific questions, which a program that merely detects facial expressions and matches them to emotions cannot do. Installing this software would cost the school a great deal of time and money without any guarantee that it would actually be useful. For these reasons, I do not believe this software would be a helpful addition for our students.

The Mona Lisa's smile is 83 percent happy, 9 percent disgusted, 6 percent fearful, and 2 percent angry. The Mona Lisa's smile shows less emotion overall because her happiness is high and not low. She has not been sad, but she has been a little mad. Her anger was 2 percent, which is low. She shows more emotion in smiling. But she is a little fearful. The Mona Lisa's smile has finally been read, according to some new computer software that can recognize her emotions. Thomas Huang, of the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science at the University of Illinois, is working in collaboration with Prof. Nicu Sebe of the University of Amsterdam. Dr. Huang and his colleagues are experts at developing better ways for humans and computers to communicate. And they were talking about calculating emotions like a math homework problem, and how computers can recognize the subtle facial movements that we humans use to express how we feel. They started by making the computer construct a 3-D computer model of the face; all 44 major muscles in the model must move like human muscles. The movement of one or more muscles is called an "action unit." Then Dr. Huang relies on the work of psychologists such as Dr. Paul Eckman, creator of FACS (the Facial Action Coding System). And according to his theory of emotion, moving your facial muscles not only expresses emotions, but may even help produce them. This may happen because we unconsciously imitate another person's facial expressions. And whoever thought that making faces could reveal so much about the science of emotions?

Well, first of all, I agree with the new technology called the Facial Action Coding System that enables computers to identify human emotions, and I think the use of the technology to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom is valuable, because some students might be having trouble managing their emotions. What I meant about students managing their emotions is that some students might be so emotional that any little thing, like when someone curses at them, makes them start crying. Using FACS (the Facial Action Coding System) to read the emotional expressions of a student can benefit how the teacher teaches, because if a student makes different expressions, like confused, bored or overwhelmed, while a teacher is teaching, it can show that what the teacher is doing is not working.

When a student shows a confused emotion, it shows that the work the teacher has given is too hard to comprehend. It shows the teacher that she has given work that is too hard for a student to understand. Given that situation, the teacher can make a plan to bring it down to the level of the grade she is teaching.

A bored student is not much good to have in a class, because when a student is bored, they tend to start disrupting the class or fall asleep in class. That shows the teacher that the way she is teaching has become too uninteresting, which should let the teacher know that she has to become more interesting and/or active so students can show more curiosity in class and get inspired to learn.

When a student becomes overwhelmed, it becomes stress, and they start to panic about all the work the teacher has given. A student being overwhelmed shows the teacher that she has given too much work or the class has become too hard to comprehend. So once the teacher knows that students have started to become overwhelmed because of her class, she has to start changing her teaching plan so students can learn better and in an easier way.

In conclusion, the classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused, bored and/or overwhelmed. That could help modify the lesson so it is effective for the human instructor. Then they are able to plan a better way to teach students, an easier and better way, so students can comprehend better.
